screens.title: Multiplayer architectures
screens.narratorSegment: Multiplayer architecture determines who holds authority and how messages travel between players. The client-server model gives a single authoritative server the power to validate inputs and maintain the canonical game state. Clients send their input to the server; the server processes physics, game rules, and state changes, then propagates updated NetworkVariable values and ClientRpc notifications to clients. This reduces cheating and makes reconciliation simpler, which is why competitive and action games favor this model. Peer-to-peer allows direct client-to-client communication, which can reduce server costs but creates problems: there is no single source of truth, making cheating and desynchronization harder to control. For many Unity projects, NGO assumes a client-server pattern where one instance can act as a host—both client and server—so you can prototype without a dedicated server. A common misconception is that peer-to-peer is always cheaper; in practice the complexity of security and consistency often makes client-server more cost-effective for reliable gameplay. Consider your game's needs: real-time competitive matches almost always require an authoritative server, while small cooperative experiences might tolerate peer-to-peer trade-offs. Multiplayer architectures means prefer server authority for security and consistent state; use host-mode for local testing and reserve p2p for limited, non-authoritative use cases.. In practical terms, client-server and peer-to-peer explained with trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Multiplayer architectures
Definition

Client-Server

A central server maintains the authoritative state. Clients send inputs; the server validates and updates state for everyone.

Strengths
  • Security and cheat prevention
  • Consistent authoritative state
  • Easier server-side validations
Weaknesses

Requires a server or host, potential cost and latency considerations depending on geography.

Definition

Peer-to-Peer (P2P)

Each client communicates directly with other clients without a central authority. This can lower server costs but raises consistency and security issues.

Use cases

Small cooperative sessions, LAN games, or prototypes where full authority isn't required.

Common misconception

P2P isn't automatically simpler; handling cheating and sync across unreliable connections often increases complexity.

Practical tip

Use host for local testing, but plan for a dedicated server for production competitive play.

Analogy

Think of the server as the referee keeping scores and rules enforced for everyone.

Check

Ask: who can write this piece of state? If many clients can, you risk desyncs and cheating.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Install & Configure
Process

Quick setup checklist

  1. Open Package Manager and install Netcode for GameObjects.
  2. Create an empty GameObject named NetworkManager and add the NetworkManager component.
  3. Add UnityTransport as the transport layer on the NetworkManager.
  4. Create a Player Prefab with a NetworkObject component and register it in NetworkManager's Network Prefabs.
  5. Assign the Player Prefab slot and test by starting Host and connecting a Client build.
Common mistakes
Forgot NetworkObject

Without NetworkObject on the prefab, spawning and ownership won't work. Add it before creating a prefab asset.

Unregistered prefab

Register the prefab in NetworkManager's list so clients can spawn it when connecting.

Transport missing

Attach UnityTransport or another supported transport to allow connections between instances.

Example check

Start Host in Editor and run a built executable as a client to verify the Player Prefab spawns on connect.

Pro tip

Use descriptive prefab names and tags to find UI elements like ScoreText for runtime updates.

Key Takeaway

A reproducible setup sequence prevents confusing spawn and permission bugs later.

screens.title: NetworkObject and prefab registration
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkObjects are the unit of synchronization in NGO. Any GameObject that must be created, destroyed, or observed across the network needs this component. When a NetworkObject is spawned by the server, NGO ensures that connected clients receive an instance of the same prefab and that ownership flags are set correctly. Register your prefab in NetworkManager so clients know how to instantiate it. Ownership determines who can perform owner-only writes to NetworkVariables and who receives certain messages. For example, assign the Player Prefab in the NetworkManager so each connecting client receives an owned instance with IsOwner true. A common mistake is modifying a prefab in the scene rather than the asset; always add NetworkObject to the prefab asset in the Project folder and register that asset. Another important practice is giving networked prefabs stable, predictable behavior: keep components that depend on local-only systems disabled for non-owner clients, and use IsOwner checks to enable local input. This prevents duplicated inputs and split responsibilities between server and client. NetworkObject and prefab registration means register networkobject prefabs in networkmanager and rely on ownership flags like isowner to control local behavior and write permissions.. In practical terms, how networkobject enables spawning, ownership, and synchronization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › NetworkObject & Prefabs
Architecture

What NetworkObject provides

  • Spawn and Despawn across clients
  • Ownership assignment (IsOwner true/false)
  • Hook points for NetworkBehaviour lifecycle callbacks like OnNetworkSpawn
Practical guidance
Register prefabs

Add the prefab asset to NetworkManager's Network Prefabs so clients can spawn copies when the server requests it.

IsOwner checks

Use IsOwner to enable input and owner-only writes, and disable local-only systems for non-owners.

Prefab vs Scene object

Modify the prefab asset and register that; editing a scene instance won't propagate to spawned clients.

Example

Assign a Cube prefab with NetworkObject as the Player Prefab so each client gets an owned cube when they connect.

Check your setup

When a client connects, does their instance log OnNetworkSpawn with IsOwner true? If not, review prefab registration.

Key Takeaway

NetworkObject and correct prefab registration are prerequisites for any synchronized multiplayer logic.

screens.title: NetworkVariable<T>
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkVariables are the primary way to synchronize frequently changing, authoritative values in NGO. They wrap basic types such as integers, vectors, and strings, and propagate changes from the server to all connected clients automatically. When you declare a NetworkVariable, you choose read and write permissions. Common patterns are ServerOnly write for authoritative values like health or global score, and OwnerOnly write for values where the owning client should update local state like a player's position. Even when an owner writes a value, the server can remain authoritative by validating changes on receipt. Clients should treat NetworkVariable updates as the source of truth for UI and remote interpolation. A frequent misconception is to use NetworkVariable for event streams like chat; discrete events are better expressed via ServerRpc and ClientRpc calls so each message can be validated and broadcast without continuously overwriting a single variable. Use OnValueChanged callbacks to react to updates, such as updating a scoreboard UI when PlayerScore changes. NetworkVariable<T> means use networkvariable for synchronized data with controlled write permissions; use rpcs for discrete events or validated actions.. In practical terms, automatic synchronization and write permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › NetworkVariable<T>
Concept

Synchronized values

NetworkVariables automatically send updated values to clients when the server (or permitted owner) writes them. They support primitive and struct types such as int, Vector3, and string.

OnValueChanged

Subscribe to changes to update UIs or trigger local effects when values change.

Permissions

Set NetworkVariableWritePermission to ServerOnly or OwnerOnly to control who can write.

Example
PlayerScore

Declare PlayerScore as ServerOnly write so only the server increments and synchronizes it to clients. Use OnValueChanged to update ScoreText UI.

Position

Use NetworkVariable<Vector3> with OwnerOnly write for owner-driven movement, with server reconciliation if needed.

Misconception

NetworkVariables are not ideal for streams of independent events like chat messages.

Pro tip

Keep payloads small and choose efficient types to reduce bandwidth use.

Key Takeaway

Treat NetworkVariables as synchronized shared state with controlled writers and callback-based updates for UIs.

screens.title: NetworkPlayer script explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simple NetworkPlayer script that synchronizes position and score. The script exposes two NetworkVariables: a Vector3 for Position and an int for PlayerScore. Position often uses OwnerOnly write permission so the owning client can update its transform locally and set the NetworkVariable; remote clients read and interpolate that value. PlayerScore typically uses ServerOnly write to prevent clients from arbitrarily changing their score. On network spawn, the script checks IsOwner: if true, it enables local input and subscribes to PlayerScore. OnValueChanged to update UI. Non-owners disable input and smoothly interpolate their transform toward Position. Value. Movement code updates Position. Value when the owner moves. When the player presses the action key to increase score, the owner calls a ServerRpc such as RequestScoreIncreaseServerRpc. The server increments PlayerScore. Value and NGO sends the new value to all clients. A common mistake is writing to ServerOnly NetworkVariables on a client; this will fail silently. Also avoid heavy physics updates on every frame across the network—use interpolation and limited update rates for smoother results and lower bandwidth. Finally, always unsubscribe from OnValueChanged in OnNetworkDespawn to avoid memory leaks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › NetworkPlayer Walkthrough
Key fields
NetworkVariable<Vector3> Position — often OwnerOnly write, clients read and interpolate.
NetworkVariable<int> PlayerScore — typically ServerOnly write, server increments score.
Use OnNetworkSpawn to enable input for owners and subscribe to OnValueChanged.
Always unsubscribe in OnNetworkDespawn to avoid leaks.
RPCs
When a client wants the server to change authoritative state, call a ServerRpc such as RequestScoreIncreaseServerRpc. The server validates and updates a NetworkVariable. For server-to-client notifications, call a ClientRpc so the server can instruct clients to play effects or sounds.
Example snippet (visual)
// Position: OwnerOnly write
public NetworkVariable<Vector3> Position = new NetworkVariable<Vector3>(writePermission: NetworkVariableWritePermission.OwnerOnly);

// Score: ServerOnly write
public NetworkVariable<int> PlayerScore = new NetworkVariable<int>(writePermission: NetworkVariableWritePermission.ServerOnly);

void Update(){ if(IsOwner){ HandleMovement(); } else { transform.position = Vector3.Lerp(transform.position, Position.Value, Time.deltaTime * 10f); } }
Misconception

Don't let clients write server-only variables. Use ServerRpc to request server actions.

Pro tip

Update position NetworkVariables at a reasonable rate and interpolate on clients to save bandwidth and improve smoothness.

Key Takeaway

Owner writes local state, server writes authoritative state. Use RPCs for discrete validated actions.

screens.title: ServerRpc and ClientRpc patterns
screens.narratorSegment: RPCs are how you express intent and notifications across machines. The typical flow begins with a client action that must be validated: the client calls a ServerRpc to inform the server about its intent, for example that it fired a weapon or picked up an item. The server receives that call, verifies conditions—did the shot actually hit? Is the item still available?—and then performs authoritative state changes such as updating a NetworkVariable or despawning a NetworkObject. If clients need to be notified of the outcome or play an effect, the server invokes a ClientRpc on the relevant clients or all clients. Use ServerRpc for client-to-server requests and ClientRpc for server-to-client broadcasts. Avoid calling ClientRpc from a client; it's not permitted. Also consider permission checks and validation on the server to prevent cheating: never trust unvalidated client input for critical gameplay. For non-critical cosmetic events, the server can still validate lightly but may choose to broadcast quicker visual cues. Design your RPCs to carry just enough data to describe the event, keep payloads small, and prefer IDs and small structs over large serialized objects.

keyIdea.text: Client → ServerRpc to request action; Server validates and updates authoritative state; Server → ClientRpc to notify or animate clients.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › RPC Patterns
Pattern

Request → Validate → Notify

Client calls ServerRpc to request an action. Server validates, updates NetworkVariables or despawns/ spawns NetworkObjects, then calls ClientRpc to notify clients.

Example flow

Client requests pickup via ServerRpc. Server checks availability, despawns the power-up, updates a NetworkVariable on the player, and calls a ClientRpc to play pickup effects.

Best practices
  • Validate all client requests on the server.
  • Keep RPC payloads minimal: use IDs and small structs.
  • Use targeted ClientRpcs to limit bandwidth when possible.
Warning

Never trust unvalidated client input for important game logic; always validate on server side.

Optimization

Batch frequent events and reduce frequency for non-essential updates to save bandwidth.

Key Takeaway

Use RPCs for discrete actions and notifications; keep server authoritative and payloads small.

screens.title: Player spawning and ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Player spawning is a predictable lifecycle: when a client connects, NetworkManager spawns the Player Prefab and assigns ownership to that client. The spawned NetworkObject will have IsOwner true for the connecting client and false for others. This ownership controls which client can write OwnerOnly NetworkVariables and which instance should enable local input. For example, you assign a Player Prefab in NetworkManager; upon successful connection the server spawns an instance and sets the newly connected client's OwnerClientId on that NetworkObject. Other clients receive the spawned instance as a remote object, so their scripts should disable local input and instead use interpolated values from NetworkVariables. If you need to transfer ownership later, NGO supports ownership change APIs, but consider security and validation: ownership transfers can allow a client to write values previously server-only, so use transfers sparingly and with checks. Always test spawning under different connection orders and reconnect scenarios to ensure consistent ownership and that no duplicate input controls remain enabled on remote instances. Player spawning and ownership means networkmanager spawns player prefab at connect, setting isowner for that client. use ownership to gate input and owner-only writes.. In practical terms, how player prefab, ownership, and isowner interact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Player Spawning & Ownership
Lifecycle
  1. Client connects to server.
  2. NetworkManager spawns the Player Prefab for that client.
  3. The spawned NetworkObject sets IsOwner true for that client's instance.
  4. Owner enables local input and can write OwnerOnly NetworkVariables.
Practical checks
Verify IsOwner

Log IsOwner in OnNetworkSpawn to confirm ownership on connect.

Disable remote input

Ensure remote instances do not process local input to avoid duplicated control.

Ownership transfer caution

If you transfer ownership later, validate the transfer to avoid exposing server-only logic to clients.

Example

When a client connects, their assigned Player instance should print Local player spawned with ClientId in OnNetworkSpawn logs.

Check

If a remote instance still accepts input, re-check IsOwner gating and disabling code paths.

Key Takeaway

Ownership is the switch that separates local control from remote observation. Respect it everywhere in your code.

screens.title: Networking challenges and mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Networking introduces common real-world challenges that affect gameplay. Latency is the delay between sending and receiving messages; use client-side prediction and server reconciliation to keep controls feeling responsive while the server remains authoritative. Bandwidth limits require you to send only necessary data: compress payloads, reduce update frequency, and prefer small data types. Jitter, which is variation in latency, can be smoothed by buffering and interpolation on the client so object motion remains stable. Packet loss means some network packets never arrive; design your important messages to be retransmitted or use reliable messaging paths for critical actions while lighter visual effects can be sent unreliably. Cheating is mitigated by having the server validate client requests and keeping authoritative logic on the server. A common mistake is trusting client-side predictions without server reconciliation; always build a fallback that the server can enforce and correct. Combined strategies—limited update rates, interpolation, and server-side validation—help you build a playable, fair multiplayer experience even on imperfect networks. Networking challenges and mitigations means latency and packet issues require prediction, interpolation, careful bandwidth use, and server validation to maintain responsiveness and fairness.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Challenges & Mitigations
Problems
  • Latency: Causes delayed reactions; use client-side prediction and reconcile with server state.
  • Bandwidth: Limit how often and how much you send; pack data tightly.
  • Jitter: Smooth variable delays with buffering and interpolation.
  • Packet loss: Rely on reliable messages for critical events or design idempotent actions.
Mitigations
Prediction & Reconcile

Make controls responsive on clients, then correct with server state to prevent drift.

Efficient updates

Send deltas, pack values, and reduce frequency for non-critical data.

Security

Keep validation and authoritative logic on the server to minimize cheating risks.

Example

Interpolate remote player positions between NetworkVariable updates to hide jitter.

Pro tip

Prioritize reliable transport for gameplay decisions, and unreliable for frequent cosmetic updates.

Key Takeaway

Combine prediction, reconciliation, and efficient messaging to keep gameplay smooth and fair on real networks.

screens.title: Build a simple multiplayer scene
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a minimal multiplayer scene that synchronizes movement and a shared score. Start a new Unity project and install Netcode for GameObjects from the Package Manager. Create a NetworkManager GameObject and attach UnityTransport. Next, create a 3D Cube named NetworkPlayer, add a NetworkObject component and the NetworkPlayer script with Position and PlayerScore NetworkVariables. Convert the cube into a prefab asset and register it under NetworkManager's Network Prefabs and assign it to the Player Prefab slot. Create a UI Text element named ScoreText and reference it from the prefab's NetworkPlayer script so OnScoreChanged updates the display. In Play, click Start Host in the Editor and run a built executable as a client. Move both players and press the action key to trigger a ServerRpc that increments the score. Observe the score update on both instances and the position interpolation for remote players. This validates your setup, NetworkVariable permissions, RPC flow, and spawning lifecycle. keyIdea.text: Assemble NGO components, register prefabs, wire UI to NetworkVariables, and verify host/client synchronization with movement and score updates.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Hands-on Activity
Setup steps
  1. Install Netcode for GameObjects via Package Manager.
  2. Create NetworkManager + attach UnityTransport.
  3. Create NetworkPlayer prefab with NetworkObject and NetworkPlayer script.
  4. Register prefab in NetworkManager and assign Player Prefab slot.
  5. Create ScoreText UI and assign to prefab's scoreText field.
  6. Start Host in Editor and run build as Client to test movement and score.
Validation checklist
  • Does OnNetworkSpawn log OwnerClientId for local player?
  • Does pressing the action key call a ServerRpc and update PlayerScore on server?
  • Does ScoreText update on both host and client via OnValueChanged?
  • Do remote players interpolate toward Position.NetworkVariable?
Example outcome

Two players move independently; pressing the action key on either increments the shared score visible on both UIs.

Troubleshoot

If prefabs don't spawn, re-check NetworkManager registration and that the prefab asset has NetworkObject attached.

Key Takeaway

A small end-to-end test verifies your entire networking flow and reveals permission or registration errors early.

screens.title: Designing networked interactions
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right synchronization primitive depends on the nature of your data. For chat messages or other discrete events, the recommended pattern is a client calling a ServerRpc to send the message to the server, which then validates and calls a ClientRpc on all clients to display the message. Using a NetworkVariable for continuous overwrites of a string is error-prone and cannot represent a stream of messages. For pickups, have the client call a ServerRpc with the power-up ID; the server validates ownership and existence, despawns the power-up NetworkObject, updates a NetworkVariable on the picking player for the effect, and optionally calls a ClientRpc to play visuals on all clients. This preserves authoritative control and ensures the state change (the power-up is gone) propagates consistently. When you design interactions, ask whether the action is continuous shared state (NetworkVariable) or a discrete event (RPC). Also consider bandwidth and whether you need reliable delivery. Structure your A P I so the client requests and the server confirms, minimizing opportunities for inconsistent state and cheating. Designing networked interactions means use serverrpc→server validation→clientrpc for events like chat and pickups; use networkvariable for shared continuous state.. In practical terms, chat messages, pickups, and the right ngo features for each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Designing Interactions
Chat example
Clients call a ServerRpc to send a message. The server validates length and content, then calls a ClientRpc on all clients to display the message. This ensures messages are sequenced and validated without relying on a continuously overwritten variable.
Why not a NetworkVariable?

A single NetworkVariable string holds only the latest value and cannot represent a stream of distinct messages reliably.

Pickup example
Client calls RequestPickupServerRpc with power-up ID. Server confirms availability, despawns the power-up NetworkObject, updates the picking player's NetworkVariable for the effect, and issues a ClientRpc to play visuals across clients.
Result

Power-up disappears for everyone and the player's effect is synchronized by authoritative state change.

Checklist

Ask: Is this an event or continuous state? Does it need server validation? Choose RPCs or NetworkVariables accordingly.

Pro tip

Use IDs and small data structures in RPCs to reduce bandwidth and simplify validation.

Key Takeaway

Match primitive types to the problem: events → RPCs, continuous shared state → NetworkVariables.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the essential concepts. First, multiplayer requires an architecture decision: client-server is server-authoritative and reduces cheating and desyncs; peer-to-peer trades authority for lower server cost but increases complexity. Second, Netcode for GameObjects gives you NetworkManager to host sessions, NetworkObject to enable spawning and ownership, and NetworkVariable to synchronize state with strict write permissions. Third, RPCs express discrete actions: clients call ServerRpc to request server work and the server calls ClientRpc to notify clients. Together, these primitives let you design reliable interactions. Keep in mind practical constraints: test by running Editor host with a client build, register your prefabs in NetworkManager, and always validate client requests on the server. These practices create consistent, testable multiplayer experiences that are resilient to network imperfections and secure against common client-side manipulations. fullNarratorScript:
Multiplayer adds a new dimension to game development: not just local logic, but shared state, authority, and communication across machines. In this chapter you'll learn the practical patterns that NGO, Unity Netcode for GameObjects, provides to make multiplayer possible: a server-authoritative model, synchronized NetworkObjects and NetworkVariables, and Remote Procedure Calls for discrete events. We'll start by clarifying the two broad architectures you will encounter, then set up a minimal project using NetworkManager and UnityTransport, and implement a simple NetworkPlayer that synchronizes position and score. As you follow along, pay attention to ownership and write permissions, because they determine which machine can update which piece of state. Finally, we'll cover common network problems like latency, bandwidth, and packet loss and suggest practical mitigations for each. By the end you will understand not only how to wire NGO into a scene, but why authoritative server logic and RPCs help keep gameplay fair and synchronized.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and use the essential building blocks of multiplayer in Unity. First, you will explain the difference between client-server and peer-to-peer architectures and why a server-authoritative model is typically preferred for competitive games. Second, you will set up a minimal project using Unity Netcode for GameObjects: install the package, add a NetworkManager, and configure UnityTransport so your sessions can start. Third, you'll use NetworkObject and NetworkVariable types to synchronize transforms and numeric state such as score, and understand write permissions so clients cannot overwrite authoritative state. Fourth, you will implement Remote Procedure Calls: a client sending a ServerRpc to request an action, and the server broadcasting with a ClientRpc. Each objective focuses on practical application: you'll run a host in the Editor, build a client, and verify synchronized movement and score updates. This will prepare you to design multiplayer logic that is secure, responsive, and testable.

This second objectives panel focuses on practical validation and common misconceptions. First, when you set up NetworkManager and prefabs, verify that your player prefab has a NetworkObject component and is registered in NetworkManager's prefab list; failing to register prefabs is a frequent setup mistake that prevents clients from spawning objects. Second, confirm NetworkVariable permissions: understand when a variable should be ServerOnly or OwnerOnly and why letting clients write authoritative state invites cheating. Third, test ServerRpc and ClientRpc flows under realistic conditions: simulate latency and packet loss to ensure the server still validates critical actions. Finally, use a simple host-and-client test: run the Editor as host and a build as client, move both players, press the action key to trigger a ServerRpc, and confirm the server updates the NetworkVariable and broadcasts changes. These checks help you move beyond code into reproducible, verifiable multiplayer behavior.

Multiplayer architecture determines who holds authority and how messages travel between players. The client-server model gives a single authoritative server the power to validate inputs and maintain the canonical game state. Clients send their input to the server; the server processes physics, game rules, and state changes, then propagates updated NetworkVariable values and ClientRpc notifications to clients. This reduces cheating and makes reconciliation simpler, which is why competitive and action games favor this model. Peer-to-peer allows direct client-to-client communication, which can reduce server costs but creates problems: there is no single source of truth, making cheating and desynchronization harder to control. For many Unity projects, NGO assumes a client-server pattern where one instance can act as a host—both client and server—so you can prototype without a dedicated server. A common misconception is that peer-to-peer is always cheaper; in practice the complexity of security and consistency often makes client-server more cost-effective for reliable gameplay. Consider your game's needs: real-time competitive matches almost always require an authoritative server, while small cooperative experiences might tolerate peer-to-peer trade-offs. Multiplayer architectures means prefer server authority for security and consistent state; use host-mode for local testing and reserve p2p for limited, non-authoritative use cases.. In practical terms, client-server and peer-to-peer explained with trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Getting the plumbing right is the first practical step. Install the Netcode for GameObjects package through the Package Manager, then add a NetworkManager GameObject to your scene. Attach UnityTransport as the transport layer so clients and hosts can connect. Next assign your Player Prefab slot later, but first create a simple 3D cube or character and add a NetworkObject component to it. Register that prefab in NetworkManager's Network Prefabs list so clients can spawn it. A frequent setup error is forgetting to register the prefab or to add NetworkObject to the prefab; that prevents clients from receiving spawned instances. After the prefab is registered, you can use NetworkManager controls to start Host, Server, or Client in the Editor. For testing, run the Editor as host and a built executable as client to see two instances connect. Each step matters: install the package, add NetworkManager, attach transport, create and NetworkObject-enable prefabs, register prefabs, and set the Player Prefab slot. Verifying each step early saves time when you later test NetworkVariables and RPCs. Install NGO and configure NetworkManager means install ngo > add networkmanager > attach unitytransport > create networkobject prefab > register prefab > assign player prefab slot > start host/client tests.. In practical terms, step-by-step project setup and common setup errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NetworkObjects are the unit of synchronization in NGO. Any GameObject that must be created, destroyed, or observed across the network needs this component. When a NetworkObject is spawned by the server, NGO ensures that connected clients receive an instance of the same prefab and that ownership flags are set correctly. Register your prefab in NetworkManager so clients know how to instantiate it. Ownership determines who can perform owner-only writes to NetworkVariables and who receives certain messages. For example, assign the Player Prefab in the NetworkManager so each connecting client receives an owned instance with IsOwner true. A common mistake is modifying a prefab in the scene rather than the asset; always add NetworkObject to the prefab asset in the Project folder and register that asset. Another important practice is giving networked prefabs stable, predictable behavior: keep components that depend on local-only systems disabled for non-owner clients, and use IsOwner checks to enable local input. This prevents duplicated inputs and split responsibilities between server and client. NetworkObject and prefab registration means register networkobject prefabs in networkmanager and rely on ownership flags like isowner to control local behavior and write permissions.. In practical terms, how networkobject enables spawning, ownership, and synchronization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NetworkVariables are the primary way to synchronize frequently changing, authoritative values in NGO. They wrap basic types such as integers, vectors, and strings, and propagate changes from the server to all connected clients automatically. When you declare a NetworkVariable, you choose read and write permissions. Common patterns are ServerOnly write for authoritative values like health or global score, and OwnerOnly write for values where the owning client should update local state like a player's position. Even when an owner writes a value, the server can remain authoritative by validating changes on receipt. Clients should treat NetworkVariable updates as the source of truth for UI and remote interpolation. A frequent misconception is to use NetworkVariable for event streams like chat; discrete events are better expressed via ServerRpc and ClientRpc calls so each message can be validated and broadcast without continuously overwriting a single variable. Use OnValueChanged callbacks to react to updates, such as updating a scoreboard UI when PlayerScore changes. NetworkVariable<T> means use networkvariable for synchronized data with controlled write permissions; use rpcs for discrete events or validated actions.. In practical terms, automatic synchronization and write permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a simple NetworkPlayer script that synchronizes position and score. The script exposes two NetworkVariables: a Vector3 for Position and an int for PlayerScore. Position often uses OwnerOnly write permission so the owning client can update its transform locally and set the NetworkVariable; remote clients read and interpolate that value. PlayerScore typically uses ServerOnly write to prevent clients from arbitrarily changing their score. RPCs are how you express intent and notifications across machines. The typical flow begins with a client action that must be validated: the client calls a ServerRpc to inform the server about its intent, for example that it fired a weapon or picked up an item. The server receives that call, verifies conditions—did the shot actually hit? Is the item still available?—and then performs authoritative state changes such as updating a NetworkVariable or despawning a NetworkObject. If clients need to be notified of the outcome or play an effect, the server invokes a ClientRpc on the relevant clients or all clients. Use ServerRpc for client-to-server requests and ClientRpc for server-to-client broadcasts. Avoid calling ClientRpc from a client; it's not permitted. Also consider permission checks and validation on the server to prevent cheating: never trust unvalidated client input for critical gameplay. For non-critical cosmetic events, the server can still validate lightly but may choose to broadcast quicker visual cues. Design your RPCs to carry just enough data to describe the event, keep payloads small, and prefer IDs and small structs over large serialized objects.

Player spawning is a predictable lifecycle: when a client connects, NetworkManager spawns the Player Prefab and assigns ownership to that client. The spawned NetworkObject will have IsOwner true for the connecting client and false for others. This ownership controls which client can write OwnerOnly NetworkVariables and which instance should enable local input. For example, you assign a Player Prefab in NetworkManager; upon successful connection the server spawns an instance and sets the newly connected client's OwnerClientId on that NetworkObject. Other clients receive the spawned instance as a remote object, so their scripts should disable local input and instead use interpolated values from NetworkVariables. If you need to transfer ownership later, NGO supports ownership change APIs, but consider security and validation: ownership transfers can allow a client to write values previously server-only, so use transfers sparingly and with checks. Always test spawning under different connection orders and reconnect scenarios to ensure consistent ownership and that no duplicate input controls remain enabled on remote instances. Networking introduces common real-world challenges that affect gameplay. Latency is the delay between sending and receiving messages; use client-side prediction and server reconciliation to keep controls feeling responsive while the server remains authoritative. Bandwidth limits require you to send only necessary data: compress payloads, reduce update frequency, and prefer small data types. Jitter, which is variation in latency, can be smoothed by buffering and interpolation on the client so object motion remains stable. Packet loss means some network packets never arrive; design your important messages to be retransmitted or use reliable messaging paths for critical actions while lighter visual effects can be sent unreliably. Cheating is mitigated by having the server validate client requests and keeping authoritative logic on the server. A common mistake is trusting client-side predictions without server reconciliation; always build a fallback that the server can enforce and correct. Combined strategies—limited update rates, interpolation, and server-side validation—help you build a playable, fair multiplayer experience even on imperfect networks. Choosing the right synchronization primitive depends on the nature of your data. For chat messages or other discrete events, the recommended pattern is a client calling a ServerRpc to send the message to the server, which then validates and calls a ClientRpc on all clients to display the message. Using a NetworkVariable for continuous overwrites of a string is error-prone and cannot represent a stream of messages. For pickups, have the client call a ServerRpc with the power-up ID; the server validates ownership and existence, despawns the power-up NetworkObject, updates a NetworkVariable on the picking player for the effect, and optionally calls a ClientRpc to play visuals on all clients. This preserves authoritative control and ensures the state change (the power-up is gone) propagates consistently. When you design interactions, ask whether the action is continuous shared state (NetworkVariable) or a discrete event (RPC). Also consider bandwidth and whether you need reliable delivery. Structure your A P I so the client requests and the server confirms, minimizing opportunities for inconsistent state and cheating. Let's consolidate the essential concepts. First, multiplayer requires an architecture decision: client-server is server-authoritative and reduces cheating and desyncs; peer-to-peer trades authority for lower server cost but increases complexity. Second, Netcode for GameObjects gives you NetworkManager to host sessions, NetworkObject to enable spawning and ownership, and NetworkVariable to synchronize state with strict write permissions. Third, RPCs express discrete actions: clients call ServerRpc to request server work and the server calls ClientRpc to notify clients. Together, these primitives let you design reliable interactions. Keep in mind practical constraints: test by running Editor host with a client build, register your prefabs in NetworkManager, and always validate client requests on the server. These practices create consistent, testable multiplayer experiences that are resilient to network imperfections and secure against common client-side manipulations.
